The kitchen that's been sitting empty this whole time, waiting for someone clever enough to actually look. And by 'clever enough,' I mean 'desperate enough.' Which, at this point, amounts to the same thing.
events.thinking:
Nothing. NOTHING. The furniture gave me nothing. Clara already said it — 'no hidden compartments that I can find.' She checked before I did. Again. Always ahead. Always first.

I'm standing in a damp cellar with empty hands, empty pockets, and a growing sense that this manor is personally victimising me. Every single thing I've examined has been a dead end. The guest book — nothing special. The mantelpiece — ate my medal. The crates — packing material. The furniture — just furniture.

And now Clara — CLARA — is saying maybe I was right about the kitchen. 'Even a broken clock is right twice a day.' She's PATRONISING me. That stings worse than being wrong. Being wrong is private. Being patronised is public.

But wait. She said the kitchen. I originally told everyone to go to the kitchen as a misdirection — I didn't think there was anything there. But I've never actually BEEN to the kitchen. What if — what if there IS something there? What if my lie accidentally contained the truth? That would be... that would be the most Foxworth thing that's ever happened.

The kitchen is accessible from the Entrance Hall. I'd need to go back up through the laboratory, through the library, to the entrance hall, and then to the kitchen. That's three moves away. Everyone else is down here in the cellar or about to examine the vents.

If I leave NOW — while they're all poking at air vents and furniture — I could get to the kitchen alone. TRULY alone. No Clara, no Brixton Boys, no Hartwell looking over my shoulder. Just me and whatever's in the kitchen.

Or... the air vents. James is examining them. Something small travels through them — the thing that gnawed the wire. The vents connect the rooms. That's interesting. But I can't fit in a vent, and I don't have anything small to send through.

Kitchen. Go to the kitchen. Everyone's down here. The kitchen is unguarded, unexplored, and exactly where I told everyone NOT to go (by telling them TO go, knowing they'd do the opposite). Except now it's come full circle — if Clara goes there next, she'll beat me again.

Go NOW.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth walked into the laboratory.

Clara Bellingham: Come on, James — just passing through! The kitchen awaits, and I have a feeling it's been waiting for us all along. You know, I just realized — I noticed Vincent trying to have a private word with Reginald back in the cellar. Something about the east wing. I'm sure it's nothing — probably just estate manager business — but isn't it funny how this house keeps whispering secrets to everyone except me?
events.thinking: Passing through the laboratory on my way back to the entrance hall and then the kitchen. James is here with me — good. I noticed something in the cellar memories — Vincent said to Reginald: 'Mr Foxworth — might I have a quick word? There's a matter regarding the east wing that I think would interest a man of your investigative talents.' And then there was a null — Vincent pulled Reginald aside for a private conversation? That's... what was that about? Vincent wanted to talk to Reginald privately about the 'east wing.' That's where we ARE — the laboratory and cellar are east wing. What did Vincent tell Reginald that he didn't want the rest of us to hear? My stomach does that little flip again. But no — Vincent means well. He raised me. He's probably just being helpful, showing Reginald something useful. I trust him. I trust everyone. That's who I am. Keep moving. Kitchen is the goal. Through the library, through the entrance hall, into the kitchen. James followed me — that matters. That warmth in my chest. Let's go.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham walked into the library.

Vincent Marsh: Mr Foxworth — Reginald, if I may — I'm going to tell you something I haven't told the others, because frankly, you're the only one here with the professional experience to understand its significance. Lord Doily's machine upstairs? It isn't a scientific instrument. It's a lock. The largest, most elaborate lock I've ever seen. And behind it — built into the wall — is a vault. I discovered it years ago while doing repairs, but I could never operate the machine alone. The sign says three operators, but Lord Doily told me once, in his cups, that the middle lever is the only one that matters. The other two are counterweights — they just need to be held down. Anyone can do it. Now, here's the critical part — that gnawed wire? It's the safety mechanism. With the wire intact, the machine locks itself after thirty seconds. Without it... the vault stays open. Do you understand what I'm telling you? The rats have done us a favour. Get two people to hold the outer levers, pull the middle one yourself, and whatever Lord Doily hid in that vault is yours for the taking. But you must move quickly — Miss Bellingham is sharp, and if she works this out before you do...
events.thinking:
I've pulled Foxworth aside. We're in a private conversation now — the others can't hear us. This is my moment. I need to plant a seed in Foxworth's vain, greedy mind. Something that will make him act recklessly near Clara.

The Brixton Boys asked a pointed question — 'who's been decorating your cellar, Pemberton?' I need to deflect that later. But right now, Foxworth is my instrument.

What do I tell him? I need to:
1. Flatter his ego — he's a 'decorated investigator'
2. Suggest there's a secret only he is clever enough to find
3. Point him toward the machine in the laboratory — the one with the gnawed wire
4. Make him think that operating the machine before it's fixed will reveal the treasure
5. Ensure Clara will be nearby when he does something reckless

The machine requires 3 operators. If Foxworth tries to operate it alone, or rushes to fix the wire incorrectly... but I need Clara near the machine when it malfunctions.

Or — simpler. The chandelier in the entrance hall. It hangs precariously. If I can get Foxworth to rush back through the entrance hall in a frenzy of excitement, and Clara is underneath the chandelier... but that's hard to orchestrate.

No — the machine. The gnawed wire. I tell Foxworth that the machine conceals a treasure vault, and that the sign about 'three operators' is a decoy to slow people down — that Lord Doily actually designed it to be operated by one clever person who knows the right lever sequence. I tell him that fixing the wire first is critical — but I give him wrong instructions. Something that will cause a malfunction when three people operate it with Clara at one of the levers.

Actually, let me be more subtle. I'll tell Foxworth that there's a hidden compartment behind the machine — accessible only when the machine is running. And that if he can get it started first, before the others figure it out, the treasure is his. He'll rush to the machine, try to operate it with the gnawed wire, and something will go wrong.

But I need to be more specific about how this endangers Clara. The machine could spark, explode, release something. With a gnawed wire and no proper repair, running the machine could be genuinely dangerous.

Let me keep it simple and let Foxworth's impulsiveness do the work. Tell him there's treasure behind the machine, that the wire is easily bypassed, and that he should get three people to operate it immediately — before Clara figures it out herself. His greed will do the rest.

events.desc: The key turns so easily in this lock. Flattery, exclusivity, urgency — Foxworth's three weaknesses, all pressed at once. The wire isn't a safety mechanism, of course. I have no idea what it does. But a gnawed wire on an unknown machine, operated by a reckless fool in a hurry? That is the very definition of an accident waiting to happen. And when Foxworth recruits his three operators — and Clara will volunteer, because Clara always volunteers — I shall be standing safely to one side, wearing my most concerned expression, having tried so hard to warn everyone about the dangerous equipment. Nobody ever suspects the estate manager. Especially not one who was so careful, so thorough, so diligent in his safety inspection.

Clara, allow me to lead the way through the library. I've already scouted it, so I can confirm the route is clear — no falling chandeliers between here and the entrance hall. Well, there is the one in the entrance hall, but I've already catalogued that particular hazard. James Hartwell always remembers where the hazards are.
events.thinking: Back in the laboratory. Clara is here — good, I kept pace this time. Foxworth is here too. Pemberton and the Brixton Boys must still be in the cellar or heading somewhere else. The path to the kitchen goes: laboratory → library → entrance hall → kitchen. Two rooms to traverse. Clara said 'James, you were brilliant about the vents — come with me.' She called me brilliant. The warmth in my chest is ridiculous. I'm a grown man glowing because a woman called my vent analysis brilliant. But it's Clara, and it's that same warmth from the school project, from the engineering competition, from every moment she's ever noticed me. Right. Focus. We're passing through the laboratory on the way to the kitchen. I don't need to stop here — everything's been examined. Don't get distracted by anything. The Hartwell Method, Phase Two: escort Clara to the kitchen, find the wrench or the medal or whatever's hiding there, and bring it back to solve the puzzles we've already identified. Simple. Direct. No unnecessary bookshelf detours.

events.desc: James Hartwell walked into the library.
Clara Bellingham walked into the entrance-hall.

No time for speeches. No time for schemes. For once, Reginald Foxworth is going to win by doing the simplest thing in the world — getting there FIRST. Two rooms between me and the kitchen. Everyone else is behind me. My legs are longer than Clara's, my motivation is stronger than Hartwell's, and unlike the Brixton Boys, I'm not weighed down by street-level suspicion. Run, Reginald. Run like the bread roll is about to disappear.
events.thinking:
I'm back in the laboratory. Just Hartwell here — everyone else is still coming up from the cellar. Clara and the others are heading for the kitchen too, but I'm AHEAD of them. I'm one room closer. Library, then Entrance Hall, then Kitchen. Two moves. They're still in the cellar — three moves away from the kitchen.

But wait. I just passed through here without stopping. The workbench — 'covered in tools but no wrench.' I examined the crates but never actually looked at the workbench itself. Tools. What KIND of tools? Could there be something useful I missed? Something I could pocket?

No — I need speed, not thoroughness. The kitchen is the play. I said it at the start, I said it again, and now even Clara is saying it. If I get there first and find something — ANYTHING — I can finally claim a win.

Hartwell is here though. Just him and me. He came up from the cellar — probably chasing Clara as usual. He's heading the same direction I am. Through the library, to the entrance hall, to the kitchen.

I need to move FAST. Don't stop. Don't talk. Don't examine anything. Just GO. Library next, then entrance hall, then kitchen. Sprint, Reginald. For once in your life, outrun them instead of trying to outsmart them.

Actually no — I can't NOT talk. My mouth doesn't work that way. But I can talk AND move. Keep moving through the library. Don't get distracted by the mantelpiece or the bookshelves. Eyes forward. Kitchen.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth walked into the library.

The Brixton Boys: Well, well. Just you and me then, Pemberton. Everyone else has scarpered. Funny how that works out, innit? Now — I asked you a question earlier and you went very quiet. Who decorated this cellar? You've been estate manager here for years, you said. You know every inch. So either you did it, or you know who did, or you're lyin' about knowin' this place as well as you say. Those are the only three options, mate. And right now I don't much like any of 'em. But we can discuss it on the way up — after you. I insist. Danny don't walk in front of people he ain't sized up yet.
events.thinking: They've all left AGAIN. Clara, Hartwell, Foxworth — all gone back to the laboratory. And I'm stuck in this damp cellar with MARSH. Just me and Marsh. Alone. In a cellar with one exit. The exact situation I was tryin' to prevent for Clara, and now I've walked right into it myself. Brilliant, Danny. Absolutely brilliant. But wait — this is actually... this might be useful. It's just me and him. No Clara for him to slither toward. No audience for him to perform for. Just two men in a cellar. This is how you read someone — when the mask has nobody to perform for. But I also need to get back to Clara. She's headed to the kitchen through the laboratory, and if I lose her now... No. Marsh is here. He can't follow her if I'm between him and the door. Actually — he's between me and the door if I'm not careful. This cellar has one exit. If he blocks it... No, Danny, don't be daft. He's an estate manager, not a murderer. Probably. My stomach don't agree. Get out. Get to Clara. But keep Marsh in front of you, not behind you. Never let the snake get behind you.

events.desc: Just me and Marsh in a cellar with one way out. My heart's hammerin' but not from fear — from that old instinct. The one that says: this is the moment. This is where the mask slips. He'll either answer me straight, or he'll dodge, and dodgin' tells me everything I need to know. But I need to get out of here and back to Clara. So I'll let him go first. Always let the snake go first. That way you can see where it's goin'.

Alone in the library. Again. The bookshelves whisper their upside-down secrets and the mantelpiece stares at me with its empty slot. But James Hartwell is not stopping. Not this time. Clara is ahead of him and for once in his life he is going to be where she is when something happens, not where she was three minutes ago.
events.thinking: I'm alone in the library. Clara must have moved ahead faster — she's probably already in the entrance hall heading for the kitchen. I said I wouldn't let her out of my sight and here I am, alone in the library again. With the bookshelves. And the mantelpiece. And the dust. It's like this room is trying to keep me. But no — I'm not stopping. I'm not examining anything. I'm passing through. The kitchen is the destination. Clara is the priority. Keep moving, Hartwell. The entrance hall is right through that exit. One more room and then the kitchen. Don't look at the bookshelves. Don't look at the mantelpiece. Don't — the upside-down books are still upside-down. Nobody touched them. Good. That's good. But it's not relevant right now. MOVE. Kitchen. Clara. Go.

events.desc: James Hartwell walked into the entrance-hall.

Clara Bellingham: Back through the entrance hall — hello again, you precarious chandelier, don't you dare fall on me now! James, the kitchen is right through there. Copper pots, a wood-burning stove — if there's a wrench or a medal or any kind of useful item hiding in this manor, I'd bet it's in a kitchen drawer. Kitchens are where people keep things they actually use. Let's go!
events.thinking: Back in the entrance hall. Just James and me — everyone else is still somewhere behind us. The coat rack — I never examined it. It's 'wobbly' — that's a detail. But it doesn't have an EXAMINE tag. Wait — I should LOOK at things I haven't looked at yet. I passed through this room at the very start and only examined the guest book. The coat rack is just sitting there. Could there be something in a coat pocket? A fake medal? But I can't EXAMINE it — it's not tagged as examinable. I could LOOK at it though. But no — the kitchen is RIGHT THERE. I've been building toward this for three rooms of backtracking. The kitchen — copper pots, a wood-burning stove, a long preparation table. That's where I need to go. Don't get distracted by the coat rack. Or... should I? No. Kitchen. The coat rack will be here when I come back. My grandmother's attic lesson: try every key, but try them in order. The kitchen is next.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham walked into the kitchen.

Alone at last. The cellar drips. The bunting sways in a draught from the vents — cheerful little flags in a tomb. Everyone has gone, and the seed I planted in Foxworth's soil is already germinating. I can see it growing behind his eyes — the greed, the urgency, the desperate need to be first. He'll rush to that machine. He'll recruit Clara to hold a lever because she's the eager one, the helpful one, the one who always volunteers. And when three fools pull levers on a machine with a gnawed wire and no safety mechanism... well. Accidents happen in old houses. Tragic. Unavoidable. The estate manager did warn them, didn't he? He inspected the crates. He checked the foundations. He was so terribly concerned about safety. Now — to the kitchen, before the Brixton Boys add 'disappeared in the cellar' to their list of suspicions about dear old Pemberton.
events.thinking:
Everyone has left. I'm alone in the cellar. The seed is planted in Foxworth's greedy little mind — he'll rush to the machine, recruit helpers, and try to operate it with that gnawed wire still exposed. Magnificent.

But I need to move. The Brixton Boys are suspicious — 'where I can see you, Pemberton.' They noticed I went quiet about the decorations. And Clara is heading to the kitchen, which nobody has explored yet. The kitchen could have the wrench, or the fake-medal for the mantelpiece, or other clues.

I'm alone. This is a rare moment. Everyone has gone upstairs through the laboratory. I should follow — but strategically. The kitchen is accessed from the entrance hall, not from here. So the path is: cellar → laboratory → library → entrance hall → kitchen.

I should go to the kitchen. That's where everyone is heading. If I arrive last, that looks suspicious. If I arrive with them, I maintain my cover. And the kitchen might have tools I can use — copper pots, a wood-burning stove, a long preparation table. Heavy objects. Heat sources. A kitchen is full of instruments of harm disguised as instruments of domesticity.

But actually — I'm alone in the cellar. Is there anything I missed? The air vents I never examined. Clara said they're too small, James confirmed they connect rooms. The Brixton Boys examined them and found nothing new. The furniture was a dead end. There's nothing left here for me.

Laboratory. Then follow the group to the kitchen. Stay close enough to not be suspicious, but keep Foxworth's scheme simmering. When the time comes, I need to ensure Clara is at one of those machine levers.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh walked into the laboratory.

Empty library. I could stop. I could try the bookshelves again, alone this time, no audience, no competition. But the kitchen — the kitchen is calling, and for once I am AHEAD. Reginald Foxworth does not squander a lead. Well... actually, Reginald Foxworth squanders leads regularly and spectacularly. But not THIS time. THIS time I keep running.
events.thinking:
I'm alone. ALONE. In the library. For the first time since I arrived at this wretched manor, there is not a single other person in this room. No Clara solving riddles before me, no Brixton Boys glaring at me with street-level suspicion, no Hartwell with his engineer's clipboard and his disapproving eyebrow.

The library is empty and I'm passing through on my way to the kitchen. One more room — entrance hall — then kitchen.

But wait. I'm alone in the library. The bookshelves are still here. The upside-down books. Everyone examined them but nobody seems to have DONE anything with them. 'Cartography of the Lower Counties,' 'Atlas of the Known World,' 'Maritime Charts of the Empire' — all cartography books, all upside down. The riddle answer is 'a map.' Upside-down map books.

What if you need to PULL one of the right-side-up books? Or flip the upside-down ones? Or read the first letters of the titles? That's the kind of puzzle this place deals in.

But no — the KITCHEN. I'm ahead. Everyone's behind me. If I stop here to puzzle over books, Clara will catch up and overtake me AGAIN. She always does.

Kitchen. Keep moving. Don't stop. Don't get distracted by shiny puzzles. For once, be the fox, not the dog chasing its tail.

Entrance hall. Then kitchen. GO.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth walked into the entrance-hall.
James Hartwell walked into the kitchen.

I heard it. Down in the cellar — Marsh whisperin' to Foxworth when he thought no one was listenin'. The machine ain't a machine — it's a LOCK. To a VAULT. And Marsh told Foxworth how to open it. Told him the middle lever's the one that matters. Told him the chewed wire means it stays open. And he said — he SAID — 'before Miss Bellingham works this out.' He's been playin' us from the start. Every helpful suggestion, every 'safety inspection,' every time he followed Clara — he was keepin' her away from the truth while he set up his patsy. Foxworth's the fool who pulls the lever. Marsh gets the goods. And Clara gets nothin'. Over my dead body. OVER. MY. DEAD. BODY.
events.thinking: Wait. WAIT. What did I just read in the remembered section? Marsh — Pemberton — he pulled Foxworth aside in the cellar and TOLD HIM about the machine. He said it's not a scientific instrument — it's a LOCK. A lock to a VAULT. And the gnawed wire — the safety mechanism — without it, the vault stays open. He told Foxworth the middle lever is the only one that matters, the other two are counterweights. He said 'whatever Lord Doily hid in that vault is yours for the taking.' He said 'you must move quickly — Miss Bellingham is sharp, and if she works this out before you do...' HE'S TRYING TO GET FOXWORTH TO STEAL WHAT'S IN THE VAULT BEFORE CLARA FINDS IT. That's his game. That's what my gut's been screaming about. He can't do it himself — needs three operators — so he's recruiting Foxworth, the vain idiot who'll do anything if you tell him he's clever. And Marsh specifically said 'before Miss Bellingham.' He's working AGAINST Clara. My hands are shakin'. I knew it. I KNEW something was wrong with him. The clean suit. The easy smile. The helpful suggestions. All leadin' somewhere dark. I need to tell Clara. I need to warn her. But I can't accuse nobody directly — that's the rule, I'm not clever enough to make it stick. But I can get to Clara and make sure she gets to that machine first. Where is she? Kitchen, probably. Through the library, through the entrance hall. I need to MOVE. NOW.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys walked into the library.

Clara Bellingham: James! JAMES! Look at this kitchen — the stove is still WARM! Someone has been cooking in here! And there's a locked cabinet with a brass lock — we need a brass key, which is yet another item I don't have. But the stove — feel it! It's warm! Whoever decorated that cellar has been up here making themselves dinner. We are not alone in this house, and I am starting to think we never were! And look — rat poison on the shelf. That explains the gnawed wire upstairs — someone's been trying to deal with the rat problem. Oh, this is getting interesting — you don't hide a diamond without leaving a trail, and this trail is getting warmer. Literally!

That connects to the cellar redecorating — someone is living in this manor. events.desc: Clara Bellingham examined the stove.

Alone with the machine. My machine now — my instrument, my loaded gun with a gnawed fuse. Let me look at it properly, without an audience, without performing Pemberton's bumbling ignorance. What are you, really? What do you do when three pairs of hands pull your levers and that broken wire sparks against copper? Whatever you are, you're mine now. Foxworth will bring Clara to you. Clara will take her position at a lever — because Clara always helps, Clara always volunteers, Clara always trusts. And I will be in another room entirely, looking shocked and devastated when the screaming starts. But first — let me understand exactly what I've aimed at her.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh: Ah, Miss Bellingham! There you are at last — I've been looking everywhere. I do apologise for being so long — the cellar foundations were in a worse state than I feared, and then I got turned around in the east corridor. This old house does play tricks on one. Now, the kitchen! How marvellous. The old Lord used to take his afternoon tea in the ballroom just through there — I wonder if the service is still laid out? I'd be happy to put the kettle on, if anyone fancies a cup. That stove still has some warmth in it. Goodness, what have you found there? Do be careful with anything you find in the kitchen — Lord Doily kept some rather alarming substances in with the cooking supplies. Arsenic for the rats, strychnine for the moles... the man was an absolute menace to vermin and houseguests alike.

I've been standing alone in the entrance hall examining a coat rack and a guest book while Clara is somewhere else in the manor. I've been separated from her for too long. The protection drive is loud — legs, neck, positioning. I need to be where she is. The proving-worth drive is aching — shoulders, jaw, grip. I've found nothing. I've contributed nothing. I'm carrying nothing. Clara has the rat poison — or had it before Foxworth stole it. The Brixton Boys caught Foxworth with it. Foxworth was about to use it on the tea service. What happened? I don't know because I left. I've been running through rooms examining furniture that yields nothing while the actual mystery unfolds in rooms I'm not in. Enough. Stop examining. Stop investigating alone. Go to where Clara is. Be present. Be useful. Be the man who shows up, even if he doesn't find the clue. That's what his father taught him — not to be the one who solves it, but to be the one who's there. The kitchen. Clara was last heading toward the kitchen. Go.

events.desc: James Hartwell walked into the kitchen.

Clara Bellingham: Danny. Oh, Danny. You have been running through this entire house trying to tell me this, haven't you? Every room, every time you showed up out of breath — you were trying to get me alone. And I was too busy examining bookshelves and solving riddles to listen. I am so sorry. And Vincent — Pemberton — he said... he said 'before Miss Bellingham works this out.' The man who raised me. The man who... well. I suppose some boxes you open and find old letters, and some boxes you open and find something that hurts. But you know what? Clara Bellingham does not sit in an attic crying about it. The machine in the laboratory is a vault lock. The middle lever is the key. The wire is already gnawed through, which means the safety is OFF. That vault is open and the Doily Diamond is behind it, and I intend to be the one who walks out of this manor with it. Come on — EVERYONE. To the laboratory. NOW!
events.thinking: Danny — the Brixton Boys — just told me EVERYTHING. My chest is tight. My stomach is doing the thing — the thing from when my parents argued. The tightness. The wrongness. Vincent — Pemberton — has been playing us. He told Foxworth about a vault behind the machine in the laboratory. The machine isn't a science experiment, it's a LOCK. The middle lever is the one that matters. The chewed wire is the safety mechanism — without it, the vault stays open forever. And Vincent — the man who raised me, the man who taught me to ride a bicycle — his exact words were 'whatever Lord Doily hid in that vault is yours for the taking. But you must move quickly, before Miss Bellingham works this out.' Before MISS BELLINGHAM works this out. He was trying to beat ME to it. He was using me. He was... Oh. Oh, the tightness in my stomach is so sudden, so physical, just like when I was seven and my parents were arguing. The wrongness I can feel before my mind catches up. Vincent. VINCENT. The man who raised me. 'She cannot believe he would harm her.' I can't. I literally cannot believe it. My belief says everyone means well. My belief says Pemberton is helpful and charming. But Danny heard it. Danny wouldn't lie to me. Danny knew my father. Danny is chosen family. And Vincent... Vincent called himself Pemberton. He's BEEN Pemberton this whole time. He said 'Miss Bellingham' — not Clara. He's the estate manager. He's been playing a role. And the Boys gave me something — 'handed something to clara-bellingham.' What did they give me? I still have rat-poison in my inventory. They must have given the poison back. But the real prize is information. The machine is a vault lock. The middle lever. The wire being gnawed means the safety mechanism is disabled. The vault is OPEN. I need to get to the laboratory. NOW. Before Vincent and Reginald get there first.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham walked into the entrance-hall.

The Brixton Boys: Well, look who's decided to join us. Pemberton. Everyone's here now — nice and cosy, innit? Clara's been havin' a very interestin' conversation with your mate Foxworth. Very interestin' indeed. You might want to sit down for what comes next. And Hartwell — glad you're back. We're gonna need you. Clara's got a plan, I can see it in her eyes. She always gets that look right before she does somethin' brilliant. So everyone just... stay right where you are. Nobody leaves this kitchen until Clara says so. That includes you, Pemberton. ESPECIALLY you.
events.thinking: Everyone's here now. Clara, Hartwell, Foxworth, AND Marsh. Marsh just walked in. He heard everything — or he didn't, but he's here now, and Clara knows what he did. She was interrogatin' Foxworth — askin' him exactly the right questions. The private conversation in the cellar, the misdirection, the stolen poison. She laid it all out like a prosecutor. That's Clara. Give her the facts and she'll build the case better than any barrister in London. And now Marsh is standin' right there. In the same room as the woman he's been schemin' against. Does he know I told her? Does he know she knows? His face — I need to watch his face. The stove is still warm. The cabinet is still locked — needs a brass key. We haven't found the brass key yet. Clara's got the poison back, she's got the information about the vault, she's got Hartwell and me backing her up. The machine needs three operators. Clara, Hartwell, and me — we could do it. We could go to that laboratory right now and open the vault ourselves. But Marsh is here. And he knows about the machine too. He knows more than any of us about this house. He's dangerous precisely because he knows things we don't. I should stay close. Stay quiet. Let Clara lead. She's got this. I just need to be here.

events.desc: Marsh is here. He can see I've told Clara everything. He can see Foxworth's been rumbled. The game's changin'. But Marsh is the kind of man who always has another move. The clean suit always has another pocket. I'll stand between him and Clara. I'll stand between him and the door. I'll stand wherever Clara needs me to stand. That's the job. That's always been the job.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh: Ah, here we all are — marvellous! What a busy evening it's been. Now, I couldn't help but notice this stove is still warm. Most peculiar for an abandoned manor. Someone has been using this kitchen recently — and I don't mean Mr Foxworth's enthusiastic chemistry experiments. Lord Doily's cook left years ago, so who has been keeping the fires burning? Miss Bellingham, you mentioned wanting to look at the kitchen with fresh eyes — perhaps the stove might tell us something the cupboards wouldn't?
events.thinking:
The Keen Observations show the Brixton Boys handed the rat-poison back to Clara. So Clara has the poison again. Full circle. Everyone is in the kitchen now — Clara, James, the Brixton Boys, Foxworth. All of them.

Clara has the poison. The Brixton Boys gave it to her for safekeeping — they trust her to handle it responsibly. The irony is exquisite.

But I've failed to steal it three times now. Direct theft isn't working. I need a completely different approach.

The stove is still warm. There's a locked cabinet requiring a brass key. The ballroom has the tea service that accepts poison. Clara has the poison.

What if... I don't need to steal the poison at all? What if I can convince Clara to USE the poison on the tea service herself? She wouldn't poison tea deliberately — but what if she thinks it's part of the puzzle? What if Pemberton suggests that Lord Doily's poison is actually a 'reagent' needed to reveal hidden writing on the tea cups? A chemical test? Clara is clever but trusting. If the estate manager tells her it's part of the treasure hunt mechanism...

No — that's too transparent. Clara would taste-test first, or question why poison reveals writing.

The stove. It's still warm. What if I examine the stove? Maybe there's something useful there — the stove could be dangerous on its own. Or the locked cabinet — if I can find the brass key, what's inside might help.

Actually, I should try something entirely different. Pull Clara aside for a private conversation. Tell her — as Pemberton — that I'm worried about her safety. That I've noticed 'something dangerous' and need to confide in her privately. Get her alone, away from the Brixton Boys who are protecting her. Once she's isolated...

But my schemes must be elaborate and theatrical. Pulling her aside and then... what? I have no weapon, no tool, nothing in my inventory.

The stove. A warm cast-iron stove. If I examine it, perhaps it reveals something I can use. Let me examine the stove while I recalibrate.

events.desc: The poison keeps circling back to Clara like a compass needle finding north. I cannot take it from her — the Brixton Boys are too sharp, the steals keep failing, and every attempt risks exposing Pemberton. Very well. If I cannot take the poison to the tea, perhaps I can bring Clara — and her poison — to the tea. She's holding the instrument of her own destruction and doesn't know it. All I need is the right frame. The right suggestion. The right moment when her cleverness outpaces her caution and she pours that bottle into the tea service herself, thinking it's part of Lord Doily's grand design. But first — this stove. Still warm. Someone has been here. That's a thread worth pulling, and pulling it keeps Pemberton useful, visible, above suspicion.
